being destitute, afflicted, tormented; <hi type="super">38</hi> (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> mountains, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> dens and caves of the earth. 39 And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise: <hi type="super">40</hi> God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect. <div eID="gen33108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33109" type="x-p"/> The apostle having given us a classis of many eminent believers, whose names are mentioned and the particular trials and actings of their faith recorded, now concludes his narrative with a more summary account of another set of believers, where the particular acts are not ascribed to particular persons by name, but left to be applied by those who are well acquainted with the sacred story; and, like a divine orator, he prefaces his part of the narrative with an elegant expostulation: <hi type="italic">What shall I say more? Time would fail me;</hi> as if he had said, "It is in vain to attempt to exhaust this subject; should I not restrain my pen, it would soon run beyond the bounds of an epistle; and therefore I shall but just mention a few more, and leave you to enlarge upon them." Observe, 1. After all our researches into the scripture, there is still more to be learned from them. 2. We must well consider in divine matters what we should say, and suit it as well as we can to the time. 3. We should be pleased to think how great the number of believers was under the Old Testament, and how strong their faith, though the objects thereof were not then so fully revealed. And, 4. We should lament it, that now, in gospel times, when the rule of faith is more clear and perfect, the number of believers should be so small and their faith so weak. <div eID="gen33109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33110" type="x-p"/> I. In this summary account the apostle mentions, <div eID="gen33110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33111" type="x-p"/> 1. Gideon, whose story we have in <reference osisRef="Judg.6.11">Judges vi. 11</reference>, &c. He was an eminent instrument raised up of God to deliver his people from the oppression of the Midianites; he was a person of mean tribe and family, called from a mean employment (threshing wheat), and saluted by an angel of God in this surprising manner, <hi type="italic">The Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of war.</hi> Gideon could not at first receive such honours, but humbly expostulates with the angel about their low and distressed state. The angel of the Lord delivers him his commission, and assures him of success, confirming the assurance by fire out of the rock. Gideon is directed to offer sacrifice, and, instructed in his duty, goes forth against the Midianites, when his army is reduced from thirty-two thousand to three hundred; yet by these, with their lamps and pitchers, God put the whole army of the Midianites to confusion and ruin: and the same faith that gave Gideon so much courage and honour enabled him to act with great meekness and modesty towards his brethren afterwards. It is the excellency of the grace of faith that, while it helps men to do great things, it keeps them from having high and great thoughts of themselves. <div eID="gen33111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33112" type="x-p"/> 2. Barak, another instrument raised up to deliver Israel out of the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Judg.4">Judges 4</reference>, where we read, (1.) Though he was a soldier, yet he received his commission and instructions from Deborah, a <hi type="italic">prophetess of the Lord;</hi> and he insisted upon having this divine oracle with him in his expedition. (2.) He obtained a great victory by his faith over all the host of Sisera. (3.) His faith taught him to return all the praise and glory to God: this is the nature of faith; it has recourse unto God in all dangers and difficulties, and then makes grateful returns to God for all mercies and deliverances. <div eID="gen33112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33113" type="x-p"/> 3. Samson, another instrument that God raised up to deliver Israel from the Philistines: his story we have in <reference osisRef="Judg.13.1-Judg.16.31">Judges xiii., xiv., xv., and xvi.</reference>, and from it we learn that the grace of faith is the strength of the soul for great service. If Samson had not had a strong faith as well as a strong arm, he had never performed such exploits. Observe, (1.) By faith the servants of God shall overcome even the roaring lion. (2.) True faith is acknowledged and accepted, even when mingled with many failings. (3.) The believer's faith endures to the end, and, in dying, gives him victory over death and all his deadly enemies; his greatest conquest he gains by dying. <div eID="gen33113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33114" type="x-p"/> 4. Jephthah, whose story we have, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.1-Judg.11.40">Judg. xi.</reference>, before that of Samson. He was raised up to deliver Israel from the Ammonites. As various and new enemies rise up against the people of God, various and new deliverers are raised up for them. In the story of Jephthah observe, (1.) The grace of God often finds out, and fastens upon, the most undeserving and ill-deserving persons, to do great things for them and by them. Jephthah was the son of a harlot. (2.) The grace of faith, wherever it is, will put men upon acknowledging God in all their ways (<reference osisRef="Judg.11.11">ch. xi. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Jephthah rehearsed all his words before the Lord in Mizpeh.</hi> (3.) The grace of faith will make men bold and venturous in a good cause. (4.) Faith will not only put men upon making their vows to God, but paying their vows after the mercy received; yea, though they have vowed to their own great grief, hurt, and loss, as in the case of Jephthah and his daughter. <div eID="gen33114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33115" type="x-p"/> 5. David, that great man after God's own heart. Few ever met with greater trials, and few ever discovered a more lively faith. His first appearance on the stage of the world was a great evidence of his faith. Having, when young, slain <hi type="italic">the lion and the bear,</hi> his faith in God encouraged him to encounter the great Goliath, and helped him to triumph over him. The same faith enabled him to bear patiently the ungrateful malice of Saul and his favourites, and to wait till God should put him into possession of the promised power and dignity. The same faith made him a very successful and victorious prince, and, after a long life of virtue and honour (though not without some foul stains of sin), he died in faith, relying upon the everlasting covenant that God had made with him and his, ordered in all things and sure; and he has left behind him such excellent memoirs of the trials and acts of faith in the book of Psalms as will ever be of great esteem and use, among the people of God. <div eID="gen33115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33116" type="x-p"/> 6. Samuel, raised up to be a most eminent prophet of the Lord to Israel, as well as a ruler over them. God revealed himself to Samuel when he was but a child, and continued to do so till his death. In his story observe, (1.) Those are likely to grow up to some eminency in faith who begin betimes in the exercise of it. (2.) Those whose business it is to reveal the mind and will of God to others had need to be well established in the belief of it themselves. <div eID="gen33116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33117" type="x-p"/> 7. To Samuel he adds, <hi type="italic">and of the prophets,</hi> who were extraordinary ministers of the Old-Testament church, employed of God sometimes to denounce judgment, sometimes to promise mercy, always to reprove sin; sometimes to foretell remarkable events, known only to God; and chiefly to give notice of the Messiah, his coming, person, and offices; for in him the prophets as well as the law center. Now a true and strong faith was very requisite for the right discharge of such an office as this. <div eID="gen33117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33118" type="x-p"/> II. Having done naming particular persons, he proceeds to tell us what things were done by their faith. He mentions some things that easily apply themselves to one or other of the persons named; but he mentions other things that are not so easy to be accommodated to any here named, but must be left to general conjecture or accommodation. <div eID="gen33118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33119" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">By faith they subdued kingdoms,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.33">v. 33</reference>. Thus did David, Joshua, and many of the judges. Learn hence, (1.) The interests and powers of kings and kingdoms are often set up in opposition to God and his people. (2.) God can easily subdue all those kings and kingdoms that set themselves to oppose him. (3.) Faith is a suitable and excellent qualification of those who fight in the ways of the Lord; it makes them just, bold, and wise. <div eID="gen33119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33120" type="x-p"/> 2. They <hi type="italic">wrought righteousness,</hi> both in their public and personal capacities; they turned many from idolatry to the ways of righteousness; they believed God, and it was imputed to them for righteousness; they walked and acted righteously towards God and man. It is a greater honour and happiness to work righteousness than to work miracles; faith is an active principle of universal righteousness. <div eID="gen33120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33121" type="x-p"/> 3. They <hi type="italic">obtained promises,</hi> both general and special. It is faith that gives us an interest in the promises; it is by faith that we have the comfort of the promises; and it is by faith that we are prepared to wait for the promises, and in due time to receive them. <div eID="gen33121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33122" type="x-p"/> 4. They <hi type="italic">stopped the mouths of lions;</hi> so did Samson, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.5-Judg.14.6">Judg. xiv. 5, 6</reference>, and David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34-1Sam.17.35">1 Sam. xvii. 34, 35</reference>, and Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.22">6.22</reference>. Here learn, (1.) The power of God is above the power of the creature. (2.) Faith engages the power of God for his people, whenever it shall be for his glory, to overcome brute beasts and brutish men. <div eID="gen33122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33123" type="x-p"/> 5. They <hi type="italic">quenched the violence of the fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.34">v. 34</reference>. So Moses, by the prayer of faith, quenched the fire of God's wrath that was kindled against the people of Israel, <reference osisRef="Num.11.1-Num.11.2">Num. xi. 1, 2</reference>. So did the three children, or rather mighty champions, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.17-Dan.3.27">Dan. iii. 17-27</reference>. Their faith in God, refusing to worship the golden image, exposed them to the fiery furnace which Nebuchadnezzar had prepared for them, and their faith engaged for them that power and presence of God in the furnace which quenched the violence of the fire, so that not so much as the smell thereof passed on them. Never was the grace of faith more severely tried, never more nobly exerted, nor ever more gloriously rewarded, than theirs was. <div eID="gen33123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33124" type="x-p"/> 6. They <hi type="italic">escaped the edge of the sword.</hi> Thus David escaped the sword of Goliath and of Saul; and Mordecai and the Jews escaped the sword of Haman. The swords of men are held in the hand of God, and he can blunt the edge of the sword, and turn it away from his people against their enemies when he pleases. Faith takes hold of that hand of God which has hold of the swords of men; and God has often suffered himself to be prevailed upon by the faith of his people. <div eID="gen33124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33125" type="x-p"/> 7. <hi type="italic">Out of weakness they were made strong.</hi> From national weakness, into which the Jews often fell by their unbelief; upon the revival of their faith, all their interest and affairs revived and flourished. From bodily weakness; thus Hezekiah, believing the word of God, recovered out of a mortal distemper, and he ascribed his recovery to the promise and power of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.15-Isa.38.16">Isa. xxxviii. 15, 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">What shall I say? He hath spoken it, and he hath also done it. Lord by these things men live, and in these is the life of my spirit.</hi> And it is the same grace of faith that from spiritual weakness helps men to recover and renew their strength. <div eID="gen33125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33126" type="x-p"/> 8. They <hi type="italic">grew valiant in fight.</hi> So did Joshua, the judges, and David. True faith gives truest courage and patience, as it discerns the strength of God, and thereby the weakness of all his enemies. And they were not only valiant, but successful. God, as a reward and encouragement of their faith, <hi type="italic">put to flight the armies of the aliens,</hi> of those who were aliens to their commonwealth, and enemies to their religion; God made them flee and fall before his faithful servants. Believing and praying commanders, at the head of believing and praying armies, have been so owned and honoured of God that nothing could stand before them. <div eID="gen33126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33127" type="x-p"/> 9. <hi type="italic">Women received their dead raised to life again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.35">v. 35</reference>. So did the widow of Zarepath (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.23">1 Kings xvii. 23</reference>), and the Shunamite, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.36">2 Kings iv. 36</reference>. (1.) <hi type="italic">In Christ there is neither male nor female;</hi> many of the weaker sex have been strong in faith. (2.) Though the covenant of grace takes in the children of believers, yet it leaves them subject to natural death. (3.) Poor mothers are loth to resign up their interest in their children, though death has taken them away. (4.) God has sometimes yielded so far to the tender affections of sorrowful women as to restore their dead children to life again. Thus Christ had compassion on the widow of Nain, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.12">Luke vii. 12</reference>, &c. (5.) This should confirm our faith in the general resurrection. <div eID="gen33127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33128" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle tells us what these believers endured by faith. 1. They <hi type="italic">were tortured, not accepting deliverance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.35">v. 35</reference>. They were put upon the rack, to make them renounce their God, their Saviour, and their religion. They bore the torture, and would not accept of deliverance upon such vile terms; and that which animated them thus to suffer was the hope they had of <hi type="italic">obtaining a better resurrection,</hi> and deliverance upon more honourable terms. This is thought to refer to that memorable story, <reference osisRef="1Mac.11.59">2 Macc. ch. vii.</reference>, &c. 2. They endured <hi type="italic">trials of cruel mockings and scourgings, and bonds and imprisonment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.36">v. 36</reference>. They were persecuted in their reputation by <hi type="italic">mockings,</hi> which are cruel to an ingenuous mind; in their persons by <hi type="italic">scourging,</hi> the punishment of slaves; in their liberty by <hi type="italic">bonds and imprisonment.</hi> Observe how inveterate is the malice that wicked men have towards the righteous, how far it will go, and what a variety of cruelties it will invent and exercise upon those against whom they have no cause of quarrel, except in the matters of their God. 3. They were put to death in the most cruel manner; some <hi type="italic">were stoned,</hi> as Zechariah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.21">2 Chron. xxiv. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">sawn asunder,</hi> as Isaiah by Manasseh. <hi type="italic">They were tempted;</hi> some read it, <hi type="italic">burnt,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Macc.7.5">2 Macc. vii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">They were slain with the sword.</hi> All sorts of deaths were prepared for them; their enemies clothed death in all the array of cruelty and terror, and yet they boldly met it and endured it. 4. Those who escaped death were used so ill that death might seem more eligible than such a life. Their enemies spared them, only to prolong their misery, and wear out all their patience; for they were forced to <hi type="italic">wander about in sheep-skins and goat-skins, being destitute, afflicted,</hi> and <hi type="italic">tormented; they wandered about in deserts, and on mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.37-Heb.11.38">v. 37, 38</reference>. They were stripped of the conveniences of life, and turned out of house and harbour. They had not raiment to put on, but were forced to cover themselves with the skins of slain beasts. They were driven out of all human society, and forced to converse with the beasts of the field, to hide themselves in dens and caves, and make their complaint to rocks and rivers, not more obdurate than their enemies. Such sufferings as these they endured then for their faith; and such they endured through the power of the grace of faith: and which shall we most admire, the wickedness of human nature, that is capable of perpetrating such cruelties on fellow creatures, or the excellency of divine grace, that is able to bear up the faithful under such cruelties, and to carry them safely through all? <div eID="gen33128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33129" type="x-p"/> IV. What they obtained by their faith. 1. A most honourable character and commendation from God, the true Judge and fountain of honour—that <hi type="italic">the world was not worthy</hi> of such men; the world did not deserve such blessings; they did not know how to value them, nor how to use them. Wicked men! The righteous are not worthy to live in the world, and God declares the world is not worthy of them; and, though they widely differ in their judgment, they agree in this, that it is not fit that good men should have their rest in this world; and therefore God receives them out of it, to that world that is suitable to them, and yet far beyond the merit of all their services and sufferings. 2. They <hi type="italic">obtained a good report</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.39">v. 39</reference>) of all good men, and of the truth itself, and have the honour to be enrolled in this sacred calendar of the Old-Testament worthies, God's witnesses; yea, they had a witness for them in the consciences of their enemies, who, while they thus abused them, were condemned by their own consciences, as persecuting those who were more righteous than themselves. 3. They obtained an interest in the promises, though not the full possession of them. They had a title to the promises, though they received not the great things promised. This is not meant of the felicity of the heavenly state, for this they did receive, when they died, in the measure of a part, in one constituent part of their persons, and the much better part; but it is meant of the felicity of the gospel-state: they had types, but not the antitype; they had shadows, but had not seen the substance; and yet, under this imperfect dispensation, they discovered this precious faith. This the apostle insists upon to render the faith more illustrious, and to provoke Christians to a holy jealousy and emulation; that they should not suffer themselves to be outdone in the exercise of faith by those who came so short of them in all the helps and advantages for believing. He tells the Hebrews that God had <hi type="italic">provided some better things for</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">v. 40</reference>), and therefore they might be assured that he expected at least as good things from them; and that since the gospel is the end and perfection of the Old Testament, which had no excellency but in its reference to Christ and the gospel, it was expected that their faith should be as much more perfect than the faith of the Old-Testament saints; for their state and dispensation were more perfect than the former, and were indeed the perfection and completion of the former, for without the gospel-church the Jewish church must have remained in an incomplete and imperfect state. This reasoning is strong, and should be effectually prevalent with us all.  <chapter eID="Heb.11"/> <div eID="gen33129" type="x-p"/>

entries.6e8236142c03f84cf88b7fc2f4284581749123e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18526"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Heb.11.1-Heb.11.40">He 11:1-40</reference>. Definition of the Faith Just Spoken of (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.39">He 10:39</reference>):</title> <div sID="gen39002" type="x-p"/> Examples from the Old Covenant for Our Perseverance in Faith.<div eID="gen39002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39003" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18526"/>1. Description of the great things which faith (in its widest sense: not here restricted to faith in the Gospel sense) does for us. Not a full definition of faith in its whole nature, but a description of its great characteristics in relation to the subject of Paul's exhortation here, namely, to perseverance.<div eID="gen39003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">substance, &c.--</hi>It substantiates promises of God which we hope for, as future in fulfilment, making them present realities to us. However, the Greek is translated in <reference osisRef="Heb.3.14">He 3:14</reference>, "confidence"; and it also here may mean "sure confidence." So Alford translates. Thomas Magister supports English Version, "The whole thing that follows is virtually contained in the first principle; now the first commencement of the things hoped for is in us through the assent of faith, which virtually contains all the things hoped for." Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Heb.6.5">He 6:5</reference>, "tasted ... powers of the world to come." Through faith, the future object of Christian hope, in its beginning, is already present. True faith infers the reality of the objects believed in and honed for (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">He 11:6</reference>). Hugo de St. Victor distinguished faith from hope. By faith alone we are sure of eternal things that they ARE: but by hope we are confident that WE SHALL HAVE them. All hope presupposes faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.25">Ro 8:25</reference>).<div eID="gen39004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evidence--</hi>"demonstration": convincing proof to the believer: the soul thereby seeing what the eye cannot see.<div eID="gen39005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things not seen--</hi>the whole invisible and spiritual world: not things future and things pleasant, as the "things hoped for," but also the past and present, and those the reverse of pleasant. "Eternal life is promised to us, but it is when we are dead: we are told of a blessed resurrection, but meanwhile we moulder in the dust; we are declared to be justified, and sin dwells in us; we hear that we are blessed, meantime we are overwhelmed in endless miseries: we are promised abundance of all goods, but we still endure hunger and thirst; God declares He will immediately come to our help, but He seems deaf to our cries. What should we do if we had not faith and hope to lean on, and if our mind did not emerge amidst the darkness above the world by the shining of the Word and Spirit of God?" [Calvin]. Faith is an assent unto truths credible upon the testimony of God (not on the reasonableness of the thing revealed, though by this we may judge as to whether it be what it professes, a genuine revelation), delivered unto us in the writings of the apostles and prophets. Thus Christ's ascension is the cause, and His absence the crown, of our faith: because He ascended, we the more believe, and because we believe in Him who hath ascended, our faith is the more accepted [Bishop Pearson]. Faith believes what it sees not; for if thou seest there is no faith; the Lord has gone away so as not to be seen: He is hidden that He may be believed; the yearning desire by faith after Him who is unseen is the preparation of a heavenly mansion for us; when He shall be seen it shall be given to us as the reward of faith [Augustine]. As Revelation deals with spiritual and invisible things exclusively, faith is the faculty needed by us, since it is the evidence of things not seen. By faith we venture our eternal interests on the bare word of God, and this is altogether reasonable. <div eID="gen39006" type="x-p"/>
entries.1465a2f4da6420797968f54d34d69bc03df4a1d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18527"/><div sID="gen39007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18527"/><hi type="bold">2. For--</hi>So high a description of faith is not undeserved; for ... [Alford].<div eID="gen39007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by it--</hi>Greek, "in it": in respect to ... in the matter of," it, "or, as Greek more emphatically, "this."<div eID="gen39008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the elders--</hi>as though still living and giving their powerful testimony to the reasonableness and excellence of faith (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>). Not merely the ancients, as though they were people solely of the past; nay, they belong to the one and the same blessed family as ourselves (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.39">He 11:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">40</reference>). "The elders," whom we all revere so highly. "Paul shows how we ought to seek in all its fulness, under the veil of history, the essential substance of the doctrine sometimes briefly indicated" [Bengel]. "The elders," as "the fathers," is a title of honor given on the ground of their bright faith and practice.<div eID="gen39009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">obtained a good report--</hi>Greek, "were testified of," namely, favorably (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.7.8">He 7:8</reference>). It is a phrase of Luke, Paul's companion. Not only men, but God, gave testimony to their faith (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.4">He 11:4</reference>, 5, 39). Thus they being testified of themselves have become "witnesses" to all others (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>). The earlier elders had their patience exercised for a long period of life: those later, in sharper afflictions. Many things which they hoped for and did not see, subsequently came to pass and were conspicuously seen, the event confirming faith [Bengel]. <div eID="gen39010" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f88bab54b24938ae62e1a5e6fd5352777ee26f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18528"/><div sID="gen39011" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18528"/><hi type="bold">3. we understand--</hi>We perceive with our spiritual intelligence the fact of the world's creation by God, though we see neither Him nor the act of creation as described in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.1-Gen.1.31">Ge 1:1-31</reference>. The natural world could not, without revelation, teach us this truth, though it confirms the truth when apprehended by faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.20">Ro 1:20</reference>). Adam is passed over in silence here as to his faith, perhaps as being the first who fell and brought sin on us all; though it does not follow that he did not repent and believe the promise.<div eID="gen39011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worlds--</hi>literally, "ages"; all that exists in time and space, visible and invisible, present and eternal.<div eID="gen39012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">framed--</hi>"fitly formed and consolidated"; including the creation of the single parts and the harmonious organization of the whole, and the continual providence which maintains the whole throughout all ages. As creation is the foundation and a specimen of the whole divine economy, so faith in creation is the foundation and a specimen of all faith [Bengel].<div eID="gen39013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the word of God--</hi>not here, the personal word (Greek, "logos," <reference osisRef="John.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference>) but the spoken word (Greek, "rhema"); though by the instrumentality of the personal word (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">He 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen39014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not made, &c.--</hi>Translate as Greek, "so that not out of things which appear hath that which is seen been made"; not as in the case of all things which we see reproduced from previously existing and visible materials, as, for instance, the plant from the seed, the animal from the parent, &c., has the visible world sprung into being from apparent materials. So also it is implied in the first clause of the verse that the invisible spiritual worlds were framed not from previously existing materials. Bengel explains it by distinguishing "appear," that is, begin to be seen (namely, at creation), from that which is seen as already in existence, not merely beginning to be seen; so that the things seen were not made of the things which appear," that is, which begin to be seen by us in the act of creation. We were not spectators of creation; it is by faith we perceive it. <div eID="gen39015" type="x-p"/>
entries.78078e23dd69a4b3e1f8d859689e9ca39d463a35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18529"/><div sID="gen39016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18529"/><hi type="bold">4. more excellent sacrifice--</hi>because offered in faith. Now faith must have some revelation of God on which it fastens. The revelation in this case was doubtless God's command to sacrifice animals ("the firstlings of the flock") in token of the forfeiture of men's life by sin, and as a type of the promised bruiser of the serpent's head (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Ge 3:15</reference>), the one coming sacrifice: this command is implied in God's having made coats of skin for Adam and Eve (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.21">Ge 3:21</reference>): for these skins must have been taken from animals slain in sacrifice: inasmuch as it was not for food they were slain, animal food not being permitted till after the flood; nor for mere clothing, as, were it so, clothes might have been made of the fleeces without the needless cruelty of killing the animal; but a coat of skin put on Adam from a sacrificed animal typified the covering or atonement (the Hebrew for atone means to cover) resulting from Christ's sacrifice. The Greek is more literally rendered [Kennicott] by Wycliffe, "a much more sacrifice"; and by Queen Elizabeth's version "a greater sacrifice." A fuller, more ample sacrifice, that which partook more largely and essentially of the true nature and virtue of sacrifice [Archbishop Magee]. It was not any intrinsic merit in "the firstling of the flock" above "the fruit of the ground." It was God's appointment that gave it all its excellency as a sacrifice; if it had not been so, it would have been a presumptuous act of will-worship (<reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>), and taking of a life which man had no right over before the flood (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.1-Gen.9.6">Ge 9:1-6</reference>). The sacrifice seems to have been a holocaust, and the sign of the divine acceptance of it was probably the consumption of it by fire from heaven (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">Ge 15:17</reference>). Hence, "to accept" a burnt sacrifice is in Hebrew "to turn it to ashes" (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.3">Psa 20:3</reference>, Margin). A flame seems to have issued from the Shekinah, or flaming cherubim, east of Eden ("the presence of the Lord," <reference osisRef="Gen.4.16">Ge 4:16</reference>), where the first sacrifices were offered. Cain, in unbelieving self-righteousness, presented merely a thank offering, not like Abel feeling his need of the propitiatory sacrifice appointed on account of sin. God "had respect (first) unto Abel, and (then) to his offering" (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.4">Ge 4:4</reference>). Faith causes the believer's person to be accepted, and then his offering. Even an animal sacrifice, though of God's appointment, would not have been accepted, had it not been offered in faith.<div eID="gen39016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he obtained witness--</hi>God by fire attesting His acceptance of him as "righteous by faith."<div eID="gen39017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his gifts--</hi>the common term for sacrifices, implying that they must be freely given.<div eID="gen39018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by it--</hi>by faith exhibited in his animal sacrifice.<div eID="gen39019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dead, yet speaketh--</hi>His blood crying front the ground to God, shows how precious, because of his "faith," he was still in God's sight, even when dead. So he becomes a witness to us of the blessed effects of faith. <div eID="gen39020" type="x-p"/>
entries.85314ecb737cc7f21c5495175fa684d70d413edd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18530"/><div sID="gen39021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18530"/>5. Faith was the ground of his pleasing God; and his pleasing God was the ground of his translation.<div eID="gen39021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">translated--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.5.22">Ge 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.5.24">24</reference>). Implying a sudden removal (the same Greek as in <reference osisRef="Gal.1.6">Ga 1:6</reference>) from mortality without death to immortality: such a CHANGE as shall pass over the living at Christ's coming (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1Co 15:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.52">52</reference>).<div eID="gen39022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">had this testimony--</hi>namely of Scripture; the Greek perfect implies that this testimony continues still: "he has been testified of."<div eID="gen39023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleased God--</hi>The Scripture testimony virtually expresses that he pleased God, namely, "Enoch walked with God." The Septuagint translates the Hebrew for "walked with God," <reference osisRef="Gen.6.9">Ge 6:9</reference>, pleased God. <div eID="gen39024" type="x-p"/>
entries.4515c90f2e70c09dc451d98a903e8c62c52d456a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18531"/><div sID="gen39025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18531"/><hi type="bold">6. without--</hi>Greek, "apart from faith": if one be destitute of faith (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.14.23">Ro 14:23</reference>).<div eID="gen39025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to please--</hi>Translate, as Alford does, the Greek aorist, "It is impossible to please God at all" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.8">Ro 8:8</reference>). Natural amiabilities and "works done before the grace of Christ are not pleasant to God, forasmuch as they spring not of faith in Jesus Christ; yea, rather, for that they are not done as God hath willed them to be done, we doubt not but they have the nature of sin" [Article XIII, Book of Common Prayer]. Works not rooted in God are splendid sins [Augustine].<div eID="gen39026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that cometh to God--</hi>as a worshipper (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.19">He 7:19</reference>).<div eID="gen39027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">must believe--</hi>once for all: Greek aorist tense.<div eID="gen39028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that God is--</hi>is the true self-existing Jehovah (as contrasted with all so-called gods, not gods, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.8">Ga 4:8</reference>), the source of all being, though he sees Him not (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.1">He 11:1</reference>) as being "invisible" (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.27">He 11:27</reference>). So Enoch; this passage implies that he had not been favored with visible appearances of God, yet he believed in God's being, and in God's moral government, as the Rewarder of His diligent worshippers, in opposition to antediluvian skepticism. Also Moses was not so favored before he left Egypt the first time (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.27">He 11:27</reference>); still he believed.<div eID="gen39029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ... is--</hi>a different Greek verb from the former "is." Translate, "is eventually"; proves to be; literally, "becomes."<div eID="gen39030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rewarder--</hi>renderer of reward [Alford]. So God proved to be to Enoch. The reward is God Himself diligently "sought" and "walked with" in partial communion here, and to be fully enjoyed hereafter. Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Ge 15:1</reference>, "I am thy exceeding great reward."<div eID="gen39031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of them--</hi>and them only.<div eID="gen39032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">diligently seek--</hi>Greek, "seek out" God. Compare "seek early," <reference osisRef="Prov.8.17">Pr 8:17</reference>. Not only "ask" and "seek," but "knock," <reference osisRef="Matt.7.7">Mt 7:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.11.12">He 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.24">Lu 13:24</reference>, "Strive" as in an agony of contest. <div eID="gen39033" type="x-p"/>
entries.645a1d3ff01be9105d24e52f479acdb8384e769f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18532"/><div sID="gen39034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18532"/><hi type="bold">7. warned of God--</hi>The same Greek, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.5">He 8:5</reference>, "admonished of God."<div eID="gen39034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">moved with fear--</hi>not mere slavish fear, but as in <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">He 5:7</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">He 5:7</reference>; Greek, "reverential fear": opposed to the world's sneering disbelief of the revelation, and self-deceiving security. Join "by faith" with "prepared an ark" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.20">1Pe 3:20</reference>).<div eID="gen39035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the which--</hi>faith.<div eID="gen39036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">condemned the world--</hi>For since he believed and was saved, so might they have believed and been saved, so that their condemnation by God is by his case shown to be just.<div eID="gen39037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness which is by faith--</hi>Greek, "according to faith." A Pauline thought. Noah is first called "righteous" in <reference osisRef="Gen.6.9">Ge 6:9</reference>. Christ calls Abel so, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">Mt 23:35</reference>. Compare as to Noah's righteousness, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.14">Eze 14:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.5">2Pe 2:5</reference>, "a preacher of righteousness." Paul here makes faith the principle and ground of his righteousness.<div eID="gen39038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heir--</hi>the consequence of sonship which flows from faith. <div eID="gen39039" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd35d3474eab39244ec16f6ea273c32694ad763a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18533"/><div sID="gen39040" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18533"/>8. From the antediluvian saints he passes to the patriarchs of Israel, to whom "the promises" belonged.<div eID="gen39040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">called--</hi>by God (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.1">Ge 12:1</reference>). The oldest manuscripts and Vulgate read, "He that was called Abraham," his name being changed from Abram to Abraham, on the occasion of God's making with him and his seed a covenant sealed by circumcision, many years after his call out of Ur. "By faith, he who was (afterwards) called Abraham (father of nations, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.5">Ge 17:5</reference>, in order to become which was the design of God's bringing him out of Ur) obeyed (the command of God: to be understood in this reading), so as to go out," &c.<div eID="gen39041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which he should after receive--</hi>He had not fully received even this promise when he went out, for it was not explicitly given him till he had reached Canaan (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.1">Ge 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.7">6, 7</reference>). When the promise of the land was given him the Canaanite was still in the land, and himself a stranger; it is in the new heaven and new earth that he shall receive his personal inheritance promised him; so believers sojourn on earth as strangers, while the ungodly and Satan lord it over the earth; but at Christ's coming that same earth which was the scene of the believer's conflict shall be the inheritance of Christ and His saints. <div eID="gen39042" type="x-p"/>
entries.be49f98be1b3651615a9f2322aedd23f2cdfcc14: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18534"/><div sID="gen39043" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18534"/><hi type="bold">9. sojourned--</hi>as a "stranger and pilgrim."<div eID="gen39043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>Greek, "into," that is, he went into it and sojourned there.<div eID="gen39044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as in a strange country--</hi>a country not belonging to him, but to others (so the Greek), <reference osisRef="Acts.7.5">Ac 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.6">6</reference>.<div eID="gen39045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelling in tabernacles--</hi>tents: as strangers and sojourners do: moving from place to place, as having no fixed possession of their own. In contrast to the abiding "city" (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.10">He 11:10</reference>).<div eID="gen39046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>Their kind of dwelling being the same is a proof that their faith was the same. They all alike were content to wait for their good things hereafter (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Lu 16:25</reference>). Jacob was fifteen years old at the death of Abraham.<div eID="gen39047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heirs with him of the same promise--</hi>Isaac did not inherit it from Abraham, nor Jacob from Isaac, but they all inherited it from God directly as "fellow heirs." In <reference osisRef="Heb.6.12">He 6:12</reference>, 15, 17, "the promise" means the thing promised as a thing in part already attained; but in this chapter "the promise" is of something still future. However, see on <reference osisRef="Heb.6.12">He 6:12</reference>. <div eID="gen39048" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd4496910a540601ba8e1f50c5d975929c262da4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18535"/><div sID="gen39049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18535"/><hi type="bold">10. looked for--</hi>Greek, "he was expecting"; waiting for with eager expectation (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.19">Ro 8:19</reference>).<div eID="gen39049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a city--</hi>Greek, "the city," already alluded to. Worldly Enoch, son of the murderer Cain, was the first to build his city here: the godly patriarchs waited for their city hereafter (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">He 11:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">12:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.14">13:14</reference>).<div eID="gen39050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foundations--</hi>Greek, "the foundations" which the tents had not, nor even men's present cities have.<div eID="gen39051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose builder and maker--</hi>Greek, "designer [Ep 1:4, 11] and master-builder," or executor of the design. The city is worthy of its Framer and Builder (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">He 11:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.2">He 8:2</reference>). Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">He 9:12</reference>, on "found." <div eID="gen39052" type="x-p"/>
entries.e688deb39f3d7759df8a4ff6d14f0ca2d905ceb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18536"/><div sID="gen39053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18536"/><hi type="bold">11. also Sara herself--</hi>though being the weaker vessel, and though at first she doubted.<div eID="gen39053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was delivered of a child--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts: then translate, "and that when she was past age" (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.19">Ro 4:19</reference>).<div eID="gen39054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she judged him faithful who had promised--</hi>after she had ceased to doubt, being instructed by the angel that it was no jest, but a matter in serious earnest. <div eID="gen39055" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf7599e0ffe0a5c0aead91316ac7000cb2150a08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18537"/><div sID="gen39056" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18537"/><hi type="bold">12. as good as dead--</hi>literally, "deadened"; no longer having, as in youth, energetic vital powers.<div eID="gen39056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stars ... sand--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Ge 22:17</reference>). <div eID="gen39057" type="x-p"/>
entries.b063808b8b21c8c066b2fe1579f3763f2c8b7de4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18538"/><div sID="gen39058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18538"/>13-16. Summary of the characteristic excellencies of the patriarchs' faith<div eID="gen39058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">died in faith--</hi>died as believers, waiting for, not actually seeing as yet their good things promised to them. They were true to this principle of faith even unto, and especially in, their dying hour (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.11.20">He 11:20</reference>).<div eID="gen39059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">These all--</hi>beginning with "Abraham" (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.8">He 11:8</reference>), to whom the promises were made (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">Ga 3:16</reference>), and who is alluded to in the end of <reference osisRef="Heb.11.13">He 11:13</reference> and in <reference osisRef="Heb.11.15">He 11:15</reference> [Bengel and Alford]. But the "ALL" can hardly but include Abel, Enoch, and Noah. Now as these did not receive the promise of entering literal Canaan, some other promise made in the first ages, and often repeated, must be that meant, namely, the promise of a coming Redeemer made to Adam, namely, "the seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent's head." Thus the promises cannot have been merely temporal, for Abel and Enoch mentioned here received no temporal promise [Archbishop Magee]. This promise of eternal redemption is the inner essence of the promises made to Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">Ga 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen39060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not having received--</hi>It was this that constituted their "faith." If they had "received" THE THING PROMISED (so "the promises" here mean: the plural is used because of the frequent renewal of the promise to the patriarchs: <reference osisRef="Heb.11.17">He 11:17</reference> says he did receive the promises, but not the thing promised), it would have been sight, not faith.<div eID="gen39061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seen them afar off--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>). Christ, as the Word, was preached to the Old Testament believers, and so became the seed of life to their souls, as He is to ours.<div eID="gen39062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and were persuaded of them--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit this clause.<div eID="gen39063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">embraced them--</hi>as though they were not "afar off," but within reach, so as to draw them to themselves and clasp them in their embrace. Trench denies that the Old Testament believers embraced them, for they only saw them afar off: he translates, "saluted them," as the homeward-bound mariner, recognizing from afar the well-known promontories of his native land. Alford translates, "greeted them." Jacob's exclamation, "I have waited for Thy salvation, O Lord" (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.18">Ge 49:18</reference>) is such a greeting of salvation from afar [Delitzsch].<div eID="gen39064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">confessed ... were strangers--</hi>so Abraham to the children of Heth (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.4">Ge 23:4</reference>); and Jacob to Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Gen.47.9">Ge 47:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.19">Psa 119:19</reference>). Worldly men hold fast the world; believers sit loose to it. Citizens of the world do not confess themselves "strangers on the earth."<div eID="gen39065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pilgrims--</hi>Greek, "temporary (literally, 'by the way') sojourners."<div eID="gen39066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on the earth--</hi>contrasted with "an heavenly" (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">He 11:16</reference>): "our citizenship is in heaven" (Greek: <reference osisRef="Heb.10.34">He 10:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.54">Psa 119:54</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>). "Whosoever professes that he has a Father in heaven, confesses himself a stranger on earth; hence there is in the heart an ardent longing, like that of a child living among strangers, in want and grief, far from his fatherland" [Luther]. "Like ships in seas while in, above the world." <div eID="gen39067" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ccd154cb44c606d949c5d2bab174cc5adb30df1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18542"/><div sID="gen39078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18542"/><hi type="bold">17. offered up--</hi>literally, "hath offered up," as if the work and its praise were yet enduring [Alford]. As far as His intention was concerned, he did sacrifice Isaac; and in actual fact "he offered him," as far as the presentation of him on the altar as an offering to God is concerned.<div eID="gen39078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tried--</hi>Greek, "tempted," as in <reference osisRef="Gen.22.1">Ge 22:1</reference>. Put to the proof of his faith. Not that God "tempts" to sin, but God "tempts" in the sense of proving or trying (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.13-Jas.1.15">Jas 1:13-15</reference>).<div eID="gen39079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39080" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>and so.<div eID="gen39080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that had received--</hi>rather as Greek, "accepted," that is, welcomed and embraced by faith, not merely "had the promises," as in <reference osisRef="Heb.7.6">He 7:6</reference>. This added to the difficulty in the way of his faith, that it was in Isaac's posterity the promises were to be fulfilled; how then could they be fulfilled if Isaac were sacrificed?<div eID="gen39081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">offered up--</hi>rather as Greek, "was offering up"; he was in the act of offering.<div eID="gen39082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his only-begotten son--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.22.2">Ge 22:2</reference>, "Take now thy son, thine only son." Eusebius [The Preparation of the Gospel, 1.10, and 4.16], has preserved a fragment of a Greek translation of Sanchoniatho, which mentions a mystical sacrifice of the Phoenicians, wherein a prince in royal robes was the offerer, and his only son was to be the victim: this evidently was a tradition derived from Abraham's offering, and handed down through Esau or Edom, Isaac's son. Isaac was Abraham's "only-begotten son" in respect of Sarah and the promises: he sent away his other sons, by other wives (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.6">Ge 25:6</reference>). Abraham is a type of the Father not sparing His only-begotten Son to fulfil the divine purpose of love. God nowhere in the Mosaic law allowed human sacrifices, though He claimed the first-born of Israel as His. <div eID="gen39083" type="x-p"/>
entries.813aede614ebe1df0e756016ac2d2b5d32c6e04b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18543"/><div sID="gen39084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18543"/><hi type="bold">18. Of whom--</hi>rather as Greek "He (Abraham, not Isaac) TO whom it was said" [Alford]. Bengel supports English Version. So <reference osisRef="Heb.1.7">He 1:7</reference> uses the same Greek preposition, "unto," for "in respect to," or "of." This verse gives a definition of the "only-begotten Son" (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.17">He 11:17</reference>).<div eID="gen39084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Isaac shall thy seed be called--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.21.12">Ge 21:12</reference>). The posterity of Isaac alone shall be accounted as the seed of Abraham, which is the heir of the promises (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.7">Ro 9:7</reference>). <div eID="gen39085" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e9c318f8abede3fb31ff1a54c15cb97d9e75d10: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18544"/><div sID="gen39086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18544"/>19. Faith answered the objections which reason brought against God's command to Abraham to offer Isaac, by suggesting that what God had promised He both could and would perform, however impossible the performance might seem (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.20">Ro 4:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen39086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">able to raise him--</hi>rather, in general, "able to raise from the dead." Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.4.17">Ro 4:17</reference>, "God who quickeneth the dead." The quickening of Sarah's dead womb suggested the thought of God's power to raise even the dead, though no instance of it had as yet occurred.<div eID="gen39087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he received him--</hi>"received him back" [Alford].<div eID="gen39088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a figure--</hi>Greek, "in a parable." Alford explains, "Received him back, risen from that death which he had undergone in, under, the figure of the ram." I prefer with Bishop Pearson, Estius, and Gregory of Nyssa, understanding the figure to be the representation which the whole scene gave to Abraham of Christ in His death (typified by Isaac's offering in intention, and the ram's actual substitution answering to Christ's vicarious death), and in His resurrection (typified by Abraham's receiving him back alive from the jaws of death, compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.9">2Co 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>); just as on the day of atonement the slain goat and the scapegoat together formed one joint rite representing Christ's death and resurrection. It was then that Abraham saw Christ's day (<reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>): accounting God was able to raise even from the dead: from which state of the dead he received him back as a type of the resurrection in Christ. <div eID="gen39089" type="x-p"/>
entries.888ab4d3afedc7422af5496b1386923ebf955ca8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18545"/><div sID="gen39090" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18545"/>20. Jacob is put before Esau, as heir of the chief, namely, the spiritual blessing.<div eID="gen39090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">concerning things to come--</hi>Greek, "even concerning things to come": not only concerning things present. Isaac, by faith, assigned to his sons things future, as if they were present. <div eID="gen39091" type="x-p"/>
entries.ddbb4392c82f87087c36f4c2a160a0780af45648: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18546"/><div sID="gen39092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18546"/><hi type="bold">21. both the sons--</hi>Greek, "each of the sons" (<reference osisRef="Gen.47.29">Ge 47:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.48.8-Gen.48.20">48:8-20</reference>). He knew not Joseph's sons, and could not distinguish them by sight, yet he did distinguish them by faith, transposing his hands intentionally, so as to lay his right hand on the younger, Ephraim, whose posterity was to be greater than that of Manasseh: he also adopted these grandchildren as his own sons, after having transferred the right of primogeniture to Joseph (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">Ge 48:22</reference>).<div eID="gen39092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and worshipped--</hi>This did not take place in immediate connection with the foregoing, but before it, when Jacob made Joseph swear that he would bury him with his fathers in Canaan, not in Egypt. The assurance that Joseph would do so filled him with pious gratitude to God, which he expressed by raising himself on his bed to an attitude of worship. His faith, as Joseph's (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.22">He 11:22</reference>), consisted in his so confidentially anticipating the fulfilment of God's promise of Canaan to his descendants, as to desire to be buried there as his proper possession.<div eID="gen39093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leaning upon the top of his staff--</hi><reference osisRef="Gen.47.31">Ge 47:31</reference>, Hebrew and English Version, "upon the bed's head." The Septuagint translates as Paul here. Jerome justly reprobates the notion of modern Rome, that Jacob worshipped the top of Joseph's staff, having on it an image of Joseph's power, to which Jacob bowed in recognition of the future sovereignty of his son's tribe, the father bowing to the son! The Hebrew, as translated in English Version, sets it aside: the bed is alluded to afterwards (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.2">Ge 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.33">49:33</reference>), and it is likely that Jacob turned himself in his bed so as to have his face toward the pillow, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.2">Is 38:2</reference> (there were no bedsteads in the East). Paul by adopting the Septuagint version, brings out, under the Spirit, an additional fact, namely, that the aged patriarch used his own (not Joseph's) staff to lean on in worshipping on his bed. The staff, too, was the emblem of his pilgrim state here on his way to his heavenly city (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.13">He 11:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.14">14</reference>), wherein God had so wonderfully supported him. <reference osisRef="Gen.32.10">Ge 32:10</reference>, "With my staff I passed over Jordan, and now I am become," &c. (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.12.11">Ex 12:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.8">Mr 6:8</reference>). In <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.47">1Ki 1:47</reference>, the same thing is said of David's "bowing on his bed," an act of adoring thanksgiving to God for God's favor to his son before death. He omits the more leading blessing of the twelve sons of Jacob; because "he plucks only the flowers which stand by his way, and leaves the whole meadow full to his readers" [Delitzsch in Alford]. <div eID="gen39094" type="x-p"/>
entries.6321ff7603e7be1aefbd24a23fb22ee1d59a2ba7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18547"/><div sID="gen39095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18547"/><hi type="bold">22. when he died--</hi>"when dying."<div eID="gen39095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the departing--</hi>"the exodus" (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.24">Ge 50:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.50.25">25</reference>). Joseph's eminent position in Egypt did not make him regard it as his home: in faith he looked to God's promise of Canaan being fulfilled and desired that his bones should rest there: testifying thus: (1) that he had no doubt of his posterity obtaining the promised land: and (2) that he believed in the resurrection of the body, and the enjoyment in it of the heavenly Canaan. His wish was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.32">Jos 24:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.16">Ac 4:16</reference>). <div eID="gen39096" type="x-p"/>
entries.10bff535d702e2e804795c44f02fd370db3afb1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18548"/><div sID="gen39097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18548"/><hi type="bold">23. parents--</hi>So the Septuagint has the plural, namely, Amram and Jochebed (<reference osisRef="Num.26.59">Nu 26:59</reference>); but in <reference osisRef="Exod.2.2">Ex 2:2</reference>, the mother alone is mentioned; but doubtless Amram sanctioned all she did, and secrecy. being their object, he did not appear prominent in what was done.<div eID="gen39097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a proper child--</hi>Greek, "a comely child." <reference osisRef="Acts.7.20">Ac 7:20</reference>, "exceeding fair," Greek, "fair to God." The "faith" of his parents in saving the child must have had some divine revelation to rest on (probably at the time of his birth), which marked their "exceeding fair" babe as one whom God designed to do a great work by. His beauty was probably "the sign" appointed by God to assure their faith.<div eID="gen39098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king's commandment--</hi>to slay all the males (<reference osisRef="Exod.1.22">Ex 1:22</reference>). <div eID="gen39099" type="x-p"/>
entries.30c8dfdd5bdad40ae629d8ad3df6646f94f81a7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18549"/><div sID="gen39100" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18549"/>24. So far from faith being opposed to Moses, he was an eminent example of it [Bengel].<div eID="gen39100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">refused--</hi>in believing self-denial, when he might possibly have succeeded at last to the throne of Egypt. Thermutis, Pharaoh's daughter, according to the tradition which Paul under the Spirit sanctions, adopted him, as Josephus says, with the consent of the king. Josephus states that when a child, he threw on the ground the diadem put on him in jest, a presage of his subsequent formal rejection of Thermutis' adoption of him. Faith made him to prefer the adoption of the King of kings, unseen, and so to choose (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.25">He 11:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.26">26</reference>) things, the very last which flesh and blood relish. <div eID="gen39101" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ca33341df7a533409d64fc199c10b7e5c27e0a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18550"/><div sID="gen39102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18550"/>25. He balanced the best of the world with the worst of religion, and decidedly chose the latter. "Choosing" implies a deliberate resolution, not a hasty impulse. He was forty years old, a time when the judgment is matured.<div eID="gen39102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a season--</hi>If the world has "pleasure" (Greek, "enjoyment") to offer, it is but "for a season." If religion bring with it "affliction," it too is but for a season; whereas its "pleasures are for evermore." <div eID="gen39103" type="x-p"/>
entries.e21699b4e59b5a938503eb483d5f5c6da700f389: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18551"/><div sID="gen39104" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18551"/><hi type="bold">26. Esteeming--</hi>Inasmuch as he esteemed.<div eID="gen39104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the reproach of Christ--</hi>that is, the reproach which falls on the Church, and which Christ regards as His own reproach, He being the Head, and the Church (both of the Old and New Testament) His body. Israel typified Christ; Israel's sufferings were Christ's sufferings (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">2Co 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.24">Col 1:24</reference>). As uncircumcision was Egypt's reproach, so circumcision was the badge of Israel's expectation of Christ, which Moses especially cherished, and which the Gentiles reproached Israel on account of. Christ's people's reproach will ere long be their great glory.<div eID="gen39105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">had respect unto, &c.--</hi>Greek, "turning his eyes away from other considerations, he fixed them on the (eternal) recompense" (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.39">He 11:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">40</reference>). <div eID="gen39106" type="x-p"/>
entries.c28a047ab22b83e8e327151707b6f9046e7ba1c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18552"/><div sID="gen39107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18552"/><hi type="bold">27. not fearing the wrath of the king--</hi>But in <reference osisRef="Exod.2.14">Ex 2:14</reference> it is said, "Moses feared, and fled from the face of Pharaoh." He was afraid, and fled from the danger where no duty called him to stay (to have stayed without call of duty would have been to tempt Providence, and to sacrifice his hope of being Israel's future deliverer according to the divine intimations; his great aim, see on <reference osisRef="Heb.11.23">He 11:23</reference>). He did not fear the king so as to neglect his duty and not return when God called him. It was in spite of the king's prohibition he left Egypt, not fearing the consequences which were likely to overtake him if he should be caught, after having, in defiance of the king, left Egypt. If he had stayed and resumed his position as adopted son of Pharaoh's daughter, his slaughter of the Egyptian would doubtless have been connived at; but his resolution to take his portion with oppressed Israel, which he could not have done had he stayed, was the motive of his flight, and constituted the "faith" of this act, according to the express statement here. The exodus of Moses with Israel cannot be meant here, for it was made, not in defiance, but by the desire, of the king. Besides, the chronological order would be broken thus, the next particular specified here, namely, the institution of the Passover, having taken place before the exodus. Besides, it is Moses' personal history and faith which are here described. The faith of the people ("THEY passed") is not introduced till <reference osisRef="Heb.11.29">He 11:29</reference>.<div eID="gen39107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">endured--</hi>steadfast in faith amidst trials. He had fled, not so much from fear of Pharaoh, as from a revulsion of feeling in finding God's people insensible to their high destiny, and from disappointment at not having been able to inspire them with those hopes for which he had sacrificed all his earthly prospects. This accounts for his strange reluctance and despondency when commissioned by God to go and arouse the people (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.15">Ex 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.4.1">4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.4.10-Exod.4.12">10-12</reference>).<div eID="gen39108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seeing him ... invisible--</hi>as though he had not to do with men, but only with God, ever before his eyes by faith, though invisible to the bodily eye (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.20">Ro 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.17">1Ti 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.16">6:16</reference>). Hence he feared not the wrath of visible man; the characteristic of faith (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.1">He 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.4">Lu 12:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen39109" type="x-p"/>
entries.49e5a162c44860aa57a3ffe541b0895e02d396e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18553"/><div sID="gen39110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18553"/><hi type="bold">28. kept--</hi>Greek, "hath kept," the Passover being, in Paul's day, still observed. His faith here was his belief in the invisible God's promise that the destroying angel should pass over, and not touch the inmates of the blood-sprinkled houses (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.23">Ex 12:23</reference>). "He acquiesced in the bare word of God where the thing itself was not apparent" [Calvin].<div eID="gen39110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the first-born--</hi>Greek neuter; both of man and beast. <div eID="gen39111" type="x-p"/>
entries.eed9965f63b42193bf06b5980b476a9bbc1eaffa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18554"/><div sID="gen39112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18554"/><hi type="bold">29. they--</hi>Moses and Israel.<div eID="gen39112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Red Sea--</hi>called so from its red seaweed, or rather from Edom (meaning "red"), whose country adjoined it.<div eID="gen39113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which ... assaying to do--</hi>Greek, "of which (Red Sea) the Egyptians having made experiment." Rashness and presumption mistaken by many for faith; with similar rash presumption many rush into eternity. The same thing when done by the believer, and when done by the unbeliever, is not the same thing [Bengel]. What was faith in Israel, was presumption in the Egyptians.<div eID="gen39114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">were drowned--</hi>Greek, "were swallowed up," or "engulfed." They sank in the sands as much as in the waves of the Red Sea. Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.15.12">Ex 15:12</reference>, "the earth swallowed them." <div eID="gen39115" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f6d0c4af05fe9cb286868f8e83e48745b41fcaf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18555"/><div sID="gen39116" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18555"/>30. The soundings of trumpets, though one were to sound for ten thousand years, cannot throw down walls, but faith can do all things [Chrysostom].<div eID="gen39116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39117" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven days--</hi>whereas sieges often lasted for years. <div eID="gen39117" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b302d614d8e7ffe0df848d66834cbc8cbfd9a5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18556"/><div sID="gen39118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18556"/>31. Rahab showed her "faith" in her confession, <reference osisRef="Josh.2.9">Jos 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>, "I know that Jehovah hath given you the land; Jehovah your God, is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath."<div eID="gen39118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the harlot--</hi>Her former life adds to the marvel of her repentance, faith, and preservation (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.31">Mt 21:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.32">32</reference>).<div eID="gen39119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believed not--</hi>Greek, "were disobedient," namely, to the will of God manifested by the miracles wrought in behalf of Israel (<reference osisRef="Josh.2.8-Josh.2.11">Jos 2:8-11</reference>).<div eID="gen39120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">received--</hi>in her house (<reference osisRef="Josh.2.1">Jos 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">4, 6</reference>).<div eID="gen39121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with peace--</hi>peaceably; so that they had nothing to fear in her house. Thus Paul, quoting the same examples (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.17">He 11:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.31">31</reference>) for the power of faith, as James (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.21">Jas 2:21</reference>, 25; see on <reference osisRef="Jas.2.21">Jas 2:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.25">Jas 2:25</reference>) does for justification by works evidentially, shows that in maintaining justification by faith alone, he means not a dead faith, but "faith which worketh by love" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Ga 5:6</reference>). <div eID="gen39122" type="x-p"/>
entries.71860bebdb19e5df3e3cdd63e343c10d1f7ac185: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18557"/><div sID="gen39123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18557"/><hi type="bold">32. the time--</hi>suitable for the length of an Epistle. He accumulates collectively some out of many examples of faith.<div eID="gen39123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gideon--</hi>put before Barak, not chronologically, but as being more celebrated. Just as Samson for the same reason is put before Jephthæ. The mention of Jephthæ as an example of "faith," makes it unlikely he sacrificed the life of his daughter for a rash vow. David, the warrior king and prophet, forms the transition from warrior chiefs to the "prophets," of whom "Samuel" is mentioned as the first. <div eID="gen39124" type="x-p"/>
entries.07df9c2e137f3c1202cdca820bef4e922d3df9fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18558"/><div sID="gen39125" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18558"/><hi type="bold">33. subdued kingdoms--</hi>as David did (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2Sa 8:1</reference>, &c.); so also Gideon subdued Midian (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.1-Judg.7.25">Jud 7:1-25</reference>).<div eID="gen39125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrought righteousness--</hi>as Samuel did (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.9">1Sa 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3-1Sam.12.23">12:3-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.33">15:33</reference>); and David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15">2Sa 8:15</reference>).<div eID="gen39126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">obtained promises--</hi>as "the prophets" (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.32">He 11:32</reference>) did; for through them the promises were given (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Da 9:21</reference>) [Bengel]. Rather, "obtained the fulfilment of promises," which had been previously the object of their faith (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.45">Jos 21:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.56">1Ki 8:56</reference>). Indeed, Gideon, Barak, &c., also obtained the things which God promised. Not "the promises," which are still future (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.13">He 11:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.39">39</reference>).<div eID="gen39127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stopped the mouths of lions--</hi>Note the words, "because he believed in his God." Also Samson (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.6">Jud 14:6</reference>), David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34-1Sam.17.37">1Sa 17:34-37</reference>), Benaiah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.20">2Sa 23:20</reference>). <div eID="gen39128" type="x-p"/>
entries.79f4c70dc6fc7d6e6555e1d11e2e46c735904773: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18559"/><div sID="gen39129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18559"/><hi type="bold">34. Quenched the violence of fire--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.3.27">Da 3:27</reference>). Not merely "quenched the fire," but "quenched the power (so the Greek) of the fire." <reference osisRef="Dan.3.19-Dan.3.30">Da 3:19-30</reference> and 6:12-23 record the last miracles of the Old Testament. So the martyrs of the Reformation, though not escaping the fire, were delivered from its having power really or lastingly to hurt them.<div eID="gen39129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">escaped ... sword--</hi>So Jephthah (<reference osisRef="Judg.12.3">Jud 12:3</reference>); and so David escaped Saul's sword (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.11">1Sa 18:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.10">19:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.12">12</reference>); Elijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.1">1Ki 19:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.14">2Ki 6:14</reference>).<div eID="gen39130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39131" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of weakness ... made strong--</hi>Samson (<reference osisRef="Judg.16.28">Jud 16:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.15.19">15:19</reference>). Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.1-Isa.38.22">Is 37:1-38:22</reference>). Milton says of the martyrs, "They shook the powers of darkness with the irresistible power of weakness."<div eID="gen39131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">valiant in fight--</hi>Barak (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.14">Jud 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.15">15</reference>). And the Maccabees, the sons of Matthias, Judas, Jonathan, and Simon, who delivered the Jews from their cruel oppressor, Antiochus of Syria.<div eID="gen39132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">armies--</hi>literally, "camps" referring to <reference osisRef="Judg.7.21">Jud 7:21</reference>. But the reference may be to the Maccabees having put to flight the Syrians and other foes. <div eID="gen39133" type="x-p"/>
entries.e19689705d1bcd38824bcbc90eebb89e6873f47e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18560"/><div sID="gen39134" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18560"/><hi type="bold">35. Women received their dead raised--</hi>as the widow of Zarephath (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.17-1Kgs.17.24">1Ki 17:17-24</reference>). The Shunammite (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.17-2Kgs.4.35">2Ki 4:17-35</reference>). The two oldest manuscripts read. "They received women of aliens by raising their dead." <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.24">1Ki 17:24</reference> shows that the raising of the widow's son by Elijah led her to the faith, so that he thus took her into fellowship, an alien though she was. Christ, in <reference osisRef="Luke.4.26">Lu 4:26</reference>, makes especial mention of the fact that Elijah was sent to an alien from Israel, a woman of Sarepta.
